Walter Mondale was the forty-second Vice President of the United States under Jimmy Carter, serving from nineteen seventy-seven to nineteen eighty-one. A veteran senator from Minnesota, Mondale embodied the values of the Great Society and New Deal liberalism during the Reagan era. Before his vice presidency, he served as U.S. Senator from Minnesota and was a leader of the Democratic Party's progressive wing, advocating for civil rights, social programs, and arms control. As Vice President, Mondale served during the Iran hostage crisis and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, during which the Carter administration took hardline stances on Cold War issues. In nineteen eighty-four, Mondale ran for president and lost forty-nine of fifty states to Ronald Reagan, winning only Minnesota and the District of Columbia. This represented the worst electoral performance by a major-party candidate since nineteen seventy-two. Notably, Mondale promised in his campaign to raise taxes, an unusual stance that contributed to his decisive defeat and became a cautionary tale in Democratic politics. After leaving office, he served as U.S. Ambassador to Japan and Norway. At age seventy-four, he ran again for Senate in two thousand two, unsuccessfully seeking his old seat. Known for his intellectual seriousness and moral clarity on civil rights and his opposition to the Vietnam War during his Senate career, Mondale remained active in elder statesman circles, advocating for progressive causes and international diplomacy well into old age.
